claim: BLOS1 is a shared subunit of BLOC-1 (biogenesis of lysosome-related organelles complex-1) and BORC (BLOC-one-related complex).
source: BLOS1 is a shared subunit of BLOC-1 (biogenesis of lysosome-related organelles complex-1) and BORC (BLOC-one-related complex) (Scott et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Scott et al., 2018.

claim: BLOC-1 is required for the biogenesis of cell-type-specific lysosome-related organelles, such as melanosomes in melanocytes and dense granules in platelets.
source: BLOC-1 is required for the biogenesis of cell-type-specific lysosome-related organelles, such as melanosomes in melanocytes and dense granules in platelets (Bowman et al., 2019; Wei and Li, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bowman et al., 2019 and Wei and Li, 2013.

claim: BORC recruits ARL8 and couples lysosomes to kinesins for anterograde transport on specific microtubule tracks.
source: BORC recruits ARL8 and couples lysosomes to kinesins for anterograde transport on specific microtubule tracks, and mediates the trafficking of synaptic vesicle precursors in neurons (Guardia et al., 2016; Niwa et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Guardia et al., 2016 and Niwa et al., 2017.

claim: BORC mediates the trafficking of synaptic vesicle precursors in neurons.
source: BORC recruits ARL8 and couples lysosomes to kinesins for anterograde transport on specific microtubule tracks, and mediates the trafficking of synaptic vesicle precursors in neurons (Guardia et al., 2016; Niwa et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Guardia et al., 2016 and Niwa et al., 2017.

claim: BLOC-1 is involved in the formation of endosomal tubular structures through cooperation with microtubule- and actin-associated machineries.
source: There is increasing evidence that BLOC-1 is involved in the formation of endosomal tubular structures through cooperation with microtubule- and actin-associated machineries (Delevoye et al., 2016; Ryder et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Delevoye et al., 2016 and Ryder et al., 2013.

claim: Constitutive knockout of Bloc1s1 in mice produces embryonic lethality.
source: Previous studies have shown that constitutive knockout of Bloc1s1 in mice produces embryonic lethality (Scott et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Scott et al., 2014 and Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: Depletion of BLOS1 leads to the destabilization of other BLOC-1 subunits.
source: Because antibody to BLOS1 was not applicable, we used two other BLOC-1 subunits (Pallidin and Dysbindin) to monitor the loss of BLOS1 as the depletion of BLOS1 leads to the destabilization of other BLOC-1 subunits (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: The content of both Pallidin and Dysbindin was significantly reduced in cKO mouse livers and hepatocytes.
source: Indeed, the content of both subunits was significantly reduced in cKO mouse livers and hepatocytes, suggesting the depletion of BLOS1 (Figure 1a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1a,b.

claim: A protein band at about 34 kD was consistently increased in plasma samples from cKO mice.
source: Although there were no changes in several abundant plasma proteins, such as albumin and transferrin, a protein band at about 34 kD was consistently increased in plasma samples from cKO mice (Figure 1f).
evidence: The claim is supported by SDS-PAGE data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Mass spectrometry identified the 34 kD protein as apolipoprotein E (ApoE).
source: Mass spectrometry identified this protein as apolipoprotein E (ApoE) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c), and immunoblotting confirmed the increase of ApoE in cKO mice plasma (Figure 1g).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Immunoblotting confirmed the increase of ApoE in cKO mice plasma.
source: Mass spectrometry identified this protein as apolipoprotein E (ApoE) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c), and immunoblotting confirmed the increase of ApoE in cKO mice plasma (Figure 1g).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: In cKO mouse plasma, VLDL level was decreased, LDL was increased, and HDL had a tendency to increase.
source: We observed that in cKO mouse plasma, VLDL level was decreased, LDL was increased, and HDL had a tendency to increase (Figure 1h).
evidence: The claim is supported by native gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 1h.

claim: There was more ApoE in the HDL slice of cKO mice.
source: Indeed, we observed that there was more ApoE in the HDL slice of cKO mice (Figure 1i).
evidence: The claim is supported by two-dimensional gel electrophoresis and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1i.

claim: LDL endocytosis in cKO hepatocytes was reduced at the initial stage.
source: We observed that LDL endocytosis in cKO hepatocytes was reduced at the initial stage (Figure 2a,b), suggesting that less LDL binds to the cell membrane of cKO hepatocytes.
evidence: The claim is supported by LDL-DiI endocytosis assay data shown in Figure 2a,b.

claim: There was a significant reduction of LDLR in cKO mouse liver.
source: We found a significant reduction of LDLR in cKO mouse liver (Figure 2c,f and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2c,f and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Immunofluorescence staining of LDLR in primary hepatocytes showed significant reduction of LDLR in cKO mice.
source: Immunofluorescence staining of LDLR in primary hepatocytes isolated from both control and cKO mice also showed significant reduction of LDLR in cKO mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Both pa mice and Kxd1-KO mice showed no obvious changes in liver LDLR levels.
source: The reduction of LDLR in cKO mouse liver was not attributable to the dysfunction of either the BLOC-1 or BORC complexes, as both the pa mice (lack of Pallidin subunit in BLOC-1) and Kxd1-KO mice (lack of KXD1 subunit in BORC) showed no obvious changes in liver LDLR levels (Figure 2d–f).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2d-f.

claim: The effect on LDLR is specific for BLOS1 alone.
source: This suggests that the effect on LDLR is specific for BLOS1 alone.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that pa and Kxd1-KO mice showed no changes in LDLR levels while cKO mice did.

claim: Reduction of LDLR was confirmed in Hep G2 cells with stable knockdown of BLOC1S1.
source: The reduction of LDLR caused by BLOS1 deficiency was further confirmed in Hep G2 cells with stable knockdown of BLOC1S1 (BLOC1S1-KD cells) (Figure 2g).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: The mRNA level of LDLR was slightly increased in BLOC1S1-KD cells.
source: The potential down-regulation effect of BLOS1 deficiency on LDLR transcriptional levels was excluded by qRT-PCR in two different sets of primers (Figure 2h) (actually, the mRNA level of LDLR was slightly increased in BLOC1S1-KD cells), suggesting a post-transcriptional effect on LDLR.
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2h.

claim: Reduction of LDLR level in BLOC1S1-KD cells was recovered after the inhibition of lysosomal degradation by leupeptin.
source: In addition, reduction of LDLR level (as well as TfR level) in BLOC1S1-KD cells was recovered after the inhibition of lysosomal degradation by leupeptin (Figure 2i), suggesting excessive degradation of LDLR or TfR due to the loss of BLOS1.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2i.

claim: The content of PCSK9 was not affected in cKO mouse livers.
source: We also noted that the content of PCSK9, a known negative regulator of LDLR degradation, was not affected in cKO mouse livers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: LDLR co-immunoprecipitated with FLAG-tagged BLOS1.
source: LDLR co-immunoprecipitated with FLAG-tagged BLOS1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d) and GST-BLOS1 fusion protein could pull-down LDLR from liver tissue lysate (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e), indicating an interaction between BLOS1 and LDLR.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d.

claim: GST-BLOS1 fusion protein could pull-down LDLR from liver tissue lysate.
source: LDLR co-immunoprecipitated with FLAG-tagged BLOS1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d) and GST-BLOS1 fusion protein could pull-down LDLR from liver tissue lysate (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e), indicating an interaction between BLOS1 and LDLR.
evidence: The claim is supported by GST pull-down data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1e.

claim: The interacting region on BLOS1 was narrowed down to residues 76–100.
source: The interacting region on BLOS1 was narrowed down to residues 76–100 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1f–h and j).
evidence: The claim is supported by GST pull-down data with BLOS1 truncations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1f-h and j.

claim: The cytosolic domain of LDLR at its C-terminus could pull down BLOS1.
source: Furthermore, the cytosolic domain of LDLR at its C-terminus could pull down BLOS1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1i,j).
evidence: The claim is supported by GST pull-down data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1i,j.

claim: Overexpressed BLOS1 with different tags all showed puncta distribution patterns in the cytosol in Hep G2 cells.
source: In Hep G2 cells, overexpressed BLOS1 with different tags all showed puncta distribution patterns in the cytosol (Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: BLOS1 partially colocalized with lysosome/MVB marker CD63.
source: We co-stained BLOS1 overexpressing cells with different organelle markers and found that BLOS1 partially colocalized with lysosome/MVB marker CD63 (Figure 3c), and almost no colocalization of BLOS1 with mitochondria (labeled by Cytochrome C) was observed (Figure 3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Almost no colocalization of BLOS1 with mitochondria was observed.
source: We co-stained BLOS1 overexpressing cells with different organelle markers and found that BLOS1 partially colocalized with lysosome/MVB marker CD63 (Figure 3c), and almost no colocalization of BLOS1 with mitochondria (labeled by Cytochrome C) was observed (Figure 3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: A small fraction of BLOS1 colocalized with the early endosome marker EEA1.
source: In addition, a small fraction of BLOS1 colocalized with the early endosome marker EEA1 (Figure 3d), and more BLOS1 puncta colocalized with TfR labeled recycling endosomes (REs) (Figure 3e) or LDLR-positive vesicles (Figure 3f, see also Figure 3g for quantification), indicating a potential role of BLOS1 in the endocytic and recycling pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: More BLOS1 puncta colocalized with TfR labeled recycling endosomes.
source: In addition, a small fraction of BLOS1 colocalized with the early endosome marker EEA1 (Figure 3d), and more BLOS1 puncta colocalized with TfR labeled recycling endosomes (REs) (Figure 3e) or LDLR-positive vesicles (Figure 3f, see also Figure 3g for quantification), indicating a potential role of BLOS1 in the endocytic and recycling pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: BLOS1 puncta colocalized with LDLR-positive vesicles.
source: In addition, a small fraction of BLOS1 colocalized with the early endosome marker EEA1 (Figure 3d), and more BLOS1 puncta colocalized with TfR labeled recycling endosomes (REs) (Figure 3e) or LDLR-positive vesicles (Figure 3f, see also Figure 3g for quantification), indicating a potential role of BLOS1 in the endocytic and recycling pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: When overexpressed in mouse primary hepatocytes, BLOS1 showed a tubular distribution in addition to the scattered puncta.
source: Interestingly, when overexpressed in mouse primary hepatocytes, BLOS1 showed a tubular distribution in addition to the scattered puncta (Figure 3h).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 3h.

claim: BLOS1 tubular structures colocalized well with α-tubulin labeled microtubules.
source: We found that these tubular structures colocalized well with α-tubulin labeled microtubules (Figure 3i, bottom) but not with actin filaments (labeled with phalloidin) (Figure 3i, top).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 3i.

claim: BLOS1 tubular structures did not colocalize with actin filaments.
source: We found that these tubular structures colocalized well with α-tubulin labeled microtubules (Figure 3i, bottom) but not with actin filaments (labeled with phalloidin) (Figure 3i, top).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 3i.

claim: BLOS1 interacted with both KIF3B and KIF13A, but not KIF16B.
source: The co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) assays revealed that BLOS1 interacted with both KIF3B and KIF13A, but not KIF16B (Figure 3j).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3j.

claim: The tubular structures that BLOS1 labeled were KIF13A-positive.
source: In agreement with these results, we found that the tubular structures that BLOS1 labeled were KIF13A-positive (Figure 3k).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 3k.

claim: LDLR mainly localized peripherally underneath the cell membrane in primary hepatocytes.
source: We noticed that LDLR mainly localized peripherally underneath the cell membrane in primary hepatocytes (Figure 4a, left), while in Hep G2 cells, LDLR showed a scattered distribution (Figure 4a, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: In Hep G2 cells, LDLR showed a scattered distribution.
source: We noticed that LDLR mainly localized peripherally underneath the cell membrane in primary hepatocytes (Figure 4a, left), while in Hep G2 cells, LDLR showed a scattered distribution (Figure 4a, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The peripherally distributed LDLR in primary hepatocytes were mostly located on clathrin-coated vesicles.
source: We found that the peripherally distributed LDLR in primary hepatocytes were mostly located on clathrin-coated vesicles (labeled by clathrin light chain A, Clta) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a), while only a portion of LDLR were colocalized with CLTA in Hep G2 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b), suggesting that LDLR in primary hepatocytes were recycled faster to the cell membrane to achieve their physiological role to recycle the majority of LDLR in plasma.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Expression of KIF13A-GFP in primary hepatocytes showed the majority of LDLR were enriched at some peripheral domains.
source: Expression of KIF13A-GFP in primary hepatocytes showed the majority of LDLR were enriched at some peripheral domains (Figure 4b), while the KIF13A truncation lacking the motor region (KIF13A-ST) retained LDLR on dispersed vesicles in the cytosol (Figure 4c), suggesting that KIF13A participates in the transport of LDLR to the cell periphery, and dysfunction of KIF13A disturbs the normal trafficking of LDLR.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: KIF13A truncation lacking the motor region retained LDLR on dispersed vesicles in the cytosol.
source: Expression of KIF13A-GFP in primary hepatocytes showed the majority of LDLR were enriched at some peripheral domains (Figure 4b), while the KIF13A truncation lacking the motor region (KIF13A-ST) retained LDLR on dispersed vesicles in the cytosol (Figure 4c), suggesting that KIF13A participates in the transport of LDLR to the cell periphery, and dysfunction of KIF13A disturbs the normal trafficking of LDLR.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: LDLR was localized to the cell periphery in full-length KIF13A-FLAG overexpressed Hep G2 cells.
source: As BLOS1 is seen on endosomal structures in Hep G2 cells (Figure 3), LDLR was localized to the cell periphery in full-length KIF13A-FLAG overexpressed Hep G2 cells, and these LDLR signals colocalized with the RE marker TfR (Figure 4d and Figure 4—source data 1), suggesting that KIF13A functions on REs during LDLR recycling.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: LDLR signals colocalized with the RE marker TfR in KIF13A-FLAG overexpressed Hep G2 cells.
source: As BLOS1 is seen on endosomal structures in Hep G2 cells (Figure 3), LDLR was localized to the cell periphery in full-length KIF13A-FLAG overexpressed Hep G2 cells, and these LDLR signals colocalized with the RE marker TfR (Figure 4d and Figure 4—source data 1), suggesting that KIF13A functions on REs during LDLR recycling.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: KIF13A-R anchored LDLR and REs on KIF13A-R positive microtubules.
source: Besides, the rigor mutant of KIF13A (KIF13A-R), an ATPase activity-lacking point mutant which binds to microtubule but is unable to move along the microtubule (Guardia et al., 2016; Nakata and Hirokawa, 1995), anchored LDLR and REs on KIF13A-R positive microtubules (Figure 4e, Figure 4—figure supplement 2a and Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4e and Figure 4—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Overexpressed full-length KIF13A elongated tubular REs.
source: In agreement with a previous report that KIF13A functions in RE tubule morphogenesis (Delevoye et al., 2014), overexpressed full-length KIF13A elongated tubular REs (labeled by EHD3), while KIF13A-ST truncation had no this effect (Figure 4f,g).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4f,g and a citation to Delevoye et al., 2014.

claim: KIF13A-ST truncation had no effect on elongating tubular REs.
source: In agreement with a previous report that KIF13A functions in RE tubule morphogenesis (Delevoye et al., 2014), overexpressed full-length KIF13A elongated tubular REs (labeled by EHD3), while KIF13A-ST truncation had no this effect (Figure 4f,g).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4f,g.

claim: The majority of actively moving Rab11A-positive recycling endosomes were also labeled by LDLR in live-cell imaging.
source: We noticed that the majority of actively moving Rab11A-positive recycling endosomes were also labeled by LDLR in live-cell imaging (Figure 4—video 3 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 4—video 3 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Expression of KIF13A-R affects the movement of REs, with most REs distributed along the KIF13A-R positive microtubules and almost static during the 2 min imaging period.
source: Live-cell imaging revealed that, in contrast to the re-distribution of REs (labeled by RAB11A) to the cell periphery by KIF13A (Figure 4—video 4), expression of KIF13A-R affects the movement of REs (labeled by RAB11A), most REs distributed along the KIF13A-R positive microtubules and were almost static during the 2 min imaging period (Figure 4h and Figure 4—figure supplement 2d and Figure 4—video 1), indicating that the LDLR anchored on microtubules through KIF13A-R on REs.
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 4h and Figure 4—figure supplement 2d.

claim: KIF13A interacted with LDLR in the co-IP assays.
source: Furthermore, we found that KIF13A interacted with LDLR in the co-IP assays (Figure 4i), and knockdown of KIF13A resembles the reduction of LDLR and TfR occurred in BLOS1 deficiency (Figure 4j).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4i.

claim: Knockdown of KIF13A resembles the reduction of LDLR and TfR occurred in BLOS1 deficiency.
source: Furthermore, we found that KIF13A interacted with LDLR in the co-IP assays (Figure 4i), and knockdown of KIF13A resembles the reduction of LDLR and TfR occurred in BLOS1 deficiency (Figure 4j).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4j.

claim: KIF3A or KIF3B was evenly distributed in cells without any enrichment of LDLR in specific regions or puncta in Hep G2 cell lines and mouse primary hepatocytes.
source: In both Hep G2 cell lines (Figure 5a) and mouse primary hepatocytes (Figure 5—source data 1), KIF3A or KIF3B was evenly distributed in cells without any enrichment of LDLR in specific regions or puncta.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The expression of KIF3B rigor mutant did not affect the cellular localization of LDLR on REs.
source: Similarly, The expression of KIF3B rigor mutant (KIF3B-R) did not affect the cellular localization of LDLR on REs (labeled by TfR) (Figure 5b).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Most of the RE puncta in KIF3B-R expressing cells were anchored at dispersed sites on KIF3B-R-positive microtubules.
source: However, by live-cell imaging analysis, we found that, unlike the active movement in control cells, most of the RE puncta in KIF3B-R expressing cells were anchored at dispersed sites on KIF3B-R-positive microtubules (Figure 5c and Figure 5—video 1), suggesting that KIF3B may play a role in the trafficking of REs.
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: BLOS1 could be recruited to microtubules by KIF3B-R.
source: In addition, we observed that BLOS1 could be recruited to microtubules by KIF3B-R, and the rigor mutants of other two KIF proteins of kinesin-2 (KIF3A or KIF3C) both had the same effect, while KIF13A-R, which also interacted with BLOS1, or KIF5B-R (a rigor mutant of a kinesin-1 component) did not affect BLOS1 localization (Figure 5d).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The rigor mutants of KIF3A or KIF3C both had the same effect of recruiting BLOS1 to microtubules.
source: In addition, we observed that BLOS1 could be recruited to microtubules by KIF3B-R, and the rigor mutants of other two KIF proteins of kinesin-2 (KIF3A or KIF3C) both had the same effect, while KIF13A-R, which also interacted with BLOS1, or KIF5B-R (a rigor mutant of a kinesin-1 component) did not affect BLOS1 localization (Figure 5d).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: KIF13A-R or KIF5B-R did not affect BLOS1 localization.
source: In addition, we observed that BLOS1 could be recruited to microtubules by KIF3B-R, and the rigor mutants of other two KIF proteins of kinesin-2 (KIF3A or KIF3C) both had the same effect, while KIF13A-R, which also interacted with BLOS1, or KIF5B-R (a rigor mutant of a kinesin-1 component) did not affect BLOS1 localization (Figure 5d).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: When KIF3A and KIF3B were co-transfected with BLOS1 in Hep G2 cells, these two KIF proteins were redistributed to BLOS1 positive puncta structures.
source: Furthermore, when KIF3A and KIF3B, which forms a heterodimer, were co-transfected with BLOS1 in Hep G2 cells, these two KIF proteins were redistributed to BLOS1 positive puncta structures (Figure 5e).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: When co-expressed with KIF3B-R or KIF3A/B heterodimer, KAP3 show similar localization pattern as BLOS1.
source: Therefore, we cloned a known kinesin-2 adaptor protein gene KAP3 and found that when co-expressed with KIF3B-R or KIF3A/B heterodimer, KAP3 show similar localization pattern as BLOS1 (Figure 5f,g), indicating that BLOS1 may act as a new adaptor protein of kinesin-2.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5f,g.

claim: KIF3A knock-down caused decreased LDLR levels in Hep G2 cells.
source: Immunoblotting assays revealed that KIF3A knock-down also caused decreased LDLR levels in Hep G2 cells (Figure 5h).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5h.

claim: The motion of anterograde transported active REs in KIF3A-KD cells was significantly different from that of control cells.
source: Further analysis revealed that the motion of anterograde transported active REs in KIF3A-KD cells was significantly different from that of control cells (Figure 6a–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 6a-d.

claim: In control cells, active REs in anterograde transport sometimes paused and then usually continued their motion in their original anterograde direction.
source: In control cells, active REs in anterograde transport sometimes paused and then usually continued their motion in their original anterograde direction (Figure 6a and Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: After the knockdown of KIF3A or BLOC1S1, active REs frequently moved backward after paused anterograde transport.
source: In contrast, after the knockdown of KIF3A (Figure 6b and Figure 6—video 1) or BLOC1S1 (Figure 6c and Figure 6—video 2), active REs frequently moved backward after paused anterograde transport.
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 6b,c.

claim: Most of the REs that moved backward after paused anterograde transport moved back to the perinuclear endocytic recycling compartment of their origin.
source: Most of these REs moved back to the perinuclear endocytic recycling compartment (ERC) of their origin by following the backward movement (Figure 6—video 1), suggesting a reduction in the percentage of REs that could eventually be destined to the cell periphery.
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 6—video 1.

claim: Unlike the successful extension to the cell periphery in control cells, most of the tips of KIF13A-positive tubules in KIF3A-KD cells showed interrupted movement when they encountered other KIF13A tubules.
source: We found that, unlike the successful extension to the cell periphery in control cells (Figure 6d and Figure 6—video 3), most of the tips of KIF13A-positive tubules in KIF3A-KD cells showed interrupted movement when they encountered other KIF13A tubules (Figure 6e and Figure 6—video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 6d,e.

claim: KIF3A-KD cells showed normal microtubule architecture.
source: In addition, KIF3A-KD cells showed normal microtubule architecture (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a) and dynamics (indicated by motility of EB1-GFP positive microtubule tips) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b and Figure 6—video 5), suggesting unaffected microtubule network after KIF3A deficiency.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a.

claim: KIF3A-KD cells showed normal microtubule dynamics.
source: In addition, KIF3A-KD cells showed normal microtubule architecture (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a) and dynamics (indicated by motility of EB1-GFP positive microtubule tips) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b and Figure 6—video 5), suggesting unaffected microtubule network after KIF3A deficiency.
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b.

claim: When KIF13A-R and KIF3B-R were co-expressed, the distribution of LDLR is determined by KIF13A-R.
source: In line with the above results, when KIF13A-R and KIF3B-R were co-expressed, the distribution of LDLR is determined by KIF13A-R, indicating that KIF13A could function upstream of KIF3B (Figure 6—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1c.

claim: When KIF3A, KIF3B, and BLOS1 were co-overexpressed to form an intact kinesin-2 complex, peripheral accumulation of LDLR which occurred in the case of KIF13A expression, was not observed.
source: However, when KIF3A, KIF3B, and BLOS1 were co-overexpressed to form an intact kinesin-2 complex, peripheral accumulation of LDLR which occurred in the case of KIF13A expression, was not observed (Figure 6—figure supplement 1d), suggesting that kinesin-2 itself may not drive the long-range anterograde transport of REs, and KIF3-BLOS1 and KIF13A may play different roles in this process.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Both KIF13A-R and KIF3B-R located on acetylated microtubules.
source: We found that both KIF13A-R and KIF3B-R located on acetylated microtubules (Figure 6—figure supplement 1e,f, top), and KIF3B-R but not KIF13A-R was additionally found on peripherally distributed tyrosinated microtubules (Figure 6—figure supplement 1e,f, bottom).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1e,f.

claim: KIF3B-R but not KIF13A-R was additionally found on peripherally distributed tyrosinated microtubules.
source: We found that both KIF13A-R and KIF3B-R located on acetylated microtubules (Figure 6—figure supplement 1e,f, top), and KIF3B-R but not KIF13A-R was additionally found on peripherally distributed tyrosinated microtubules (Figure 6—figure supplement 1e,f, bottom).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1e,f.

claim: After knockdown of KIF3A, when encountering other KIF13A-GFP positive tubules, tips of KIF13A tubules were unable to pass through and move on.
source: We found that, after knockdown of KIF3A, when encountering other KIF13A-GFP positive tubules, tips of KIF13A tubules were unable to pass through and move on (Figure 7a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 7a,b.

claim: A certain percentage of BLOS1 puncta (77.6 ± 4.6%, n = 8 cells, mean ± SD) located at the intersections of microtubules in Hep G2 cells.
source: To test this idea, we first detected the distribution of BLOS1 on microtubules using super-resolution microscopy and found that a certain percentage of BLOS1 puncta (77.6 ± 4.6%, n = 8 cells, mean ± SD) located at the intersections of microtubules in Hep G2 cells (Figure 7c, see also Figure 7—video 1 for z-stack reconstruction movie), which could also be observed in mouse primary hepatocytes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a,b), indicating that kinesin-2 may function at these sites.
evidence: The claim is supported by super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 7c.

claim: A large proportion of pausing events of recycling endosomes occurred at microtubule intersection sites.
source: We found that a large proportion of pausing events of recycling endosomes occurred at microtubule intersection sites, and in most cases, recycling endosomes moved on without changing their motion polarity after the pausing (Figure 7—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 7—video 2.

claim: In most cases, recycling endosomes moved on without changing their motion polarity after pausing at microtubule intersection sites.
source: We found that a large proportion of pausing events of recycling endosomes occurred at microtubule intersection sites, and in most cases, recycling endosomes moved on without changing their motion polarity after the pausing (Figure 7—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 7—video 2.

claim: The frequency of reversed movement of recycling endosomes after paused anterograde transport at specific microtubule intersections was increased by knockdown of either BLOC1S1 (77.3 ± 8.4%) or KIF3A (78.7 ± 6.6%) as compared to control cells (10.1 ± 1.8%).
source: Furthermore, statistic results showed that the frequency of reversed movement of recycling endosomes after paused anterograde transport at specific microtubule intersections was increased by knockdown of either BLOC1S1 (77.3 ± 8.4%) or KIF3A (78.7 ± 6.6%) as compared to control cells (10.1 ± 1.8%) (Figure 7d), suggesting that dysfunction of BLOS1-dependent kinesin-2 complex alters the behavior of recycling endosomes at specific microtubule intersections by changing their motion polarity and finally reduces the recycling of LDLR.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: BLOS1 acts as an adaptor for kinesin-2 to assist the LDLR cargo transportation driven by kinesin-3 at specific microtubule-microtubule intersections.
source: In summary, our observations suggest that BLOS1 acts as an adaptor for kinesin-2 to assist the LDLR cargo transportation driven by kinesin-3 at specific microtubule-microtubule intersections where hurdles may preclude the cargo for smooth long-range anterograde transport (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is a summary inference based on multiple experimental observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: LDLR in hepatocytes plays a key role in plasma clearance of circulating LDL and in whole body cholesterol homeostasis.
source: Low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) in hepatocytes plays a key role in plasma clearance of circulating LDL and in whole body cholesterol homeostasis.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Loss of BLOS1 leads to less membrane LDLR and impairs LDL clearance from plasma in hepatocyte-specific BLOS1 knockout mice.
source: Loss of BLOS1 leads to less membrane LDLR and impairs LDL clearance from plasma in hepatocyte-specific BLOS1 knockout mice.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: BLOS1 interacts with kinesin-3 motor KIF13A.
source: BLOS1 interacts with kinesin-3 motor KIF13A, and BLOS1 acts as a new adaptor for kinesin-2 motor KIF3 to coordinate kinesin-3 and kinesin-2 during the long-range transport of recycling endosomes (REs) to plasma membrane along microtubule tracks to overcome hurdles at microtubule intersections.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: BLOS1 acts as a new adaptor for kinesin-2 motor KIF3 to coordinate kinesin-3 and kinesin-2 during the long-range transport of recycling endosomes to plasma membrane along microtubule tracks.
source: BLOS1 interacts with kinesin-3 motor KIF13A, and BLOS1 acts as a new adaptor for kinesin-2 motor KIF3 to coordinate kinesin-3 and kinesin-2 during the long-range transport of recycling endosomes (REs) to plasma membrane along microtubule tracks to overcome hurdles at microtubule intersections.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by multiple experimental observations.

claim: LDLR is essential for cellular uptake of cholesterol-carrying low-density lipoproteins and plays a crucial role in cholesterol homeostasis in mammals.
source: Low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) is essential for cellular uptake of cholesterol-carrying low-density lipoproteins (LDL) and plays a crucial role in cholesterol homeostasis in mammals (Goldstein and Brown, 2009; Goldstein and Brown, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Goldstein and Brown, 2009 and 2015.

claim: After the binding of LDL on the cell surface, LDLR enters early endosomes through clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
source: After the binding of LDL on the cell surface, LDLR enters early endosomes through clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME) and is further recycled to the cell membrane by the RAB4-dependent fast recycling pathway or the RAB11A-dependent slow recycling pathway (Ullrich et al., 1996; van der Sluijs et al., 1992; Wijers et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ullrich et al., 1996, van der Sluijs et al., 1992, and Wijers et al., 2015.

claim: LDLR is further recycled to the cell membrane by the RAB4-dependent fast recycling pathway or the RAB11A-dependent slow recycling pathway.
source: After the binding of LDL on the cell surface, LDLR enters early endosomes through clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME) and is further recycled to the cell membrane by the RAB4-dependent fast recycling pathway or the RAB11A-dependent slow recycling pathway (Ullrich et al., 1996; van der Sluijs et al., 1992; Wijers et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ullrich et al., 1996, van der Sluijs et al., 1992, and Wijers et al., 2015.

claim: In the slow recycling pathway, receptors are first sorted into the perinuclear endocytic recycling compartment and then transported to the cell periphery by recycling endosomes.
source: In the slow recycling pathway, receptors are first sorted into the perinuclear endocytic recycling compartment (ERC) and then transported to the cell periphery by recycling endosomes (REs) (Naslavsky and Caplan, 2018; Yamashiro et al., 1984).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Naslavsky and Caplan, 2018 and Yamashiro et al., 1984.

claim: RAB11A effectors (RAB11-FIPs) and Eps15-homology domain-containing proteins (EHDs) participate in the trafficking from early endosome to the ERC.
source: Factors including RAB11A effectors (RAB11-FIPs) and Eps15-homology domain-containing proteins (EHDs) participate in the trafficking from early endosome (EE) to the ERC (Horgan and McCaffrey, 2009; Naslavsky and Caplan, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Horgan and McCaffrey, 2009 and Naslavsky and Caplan, 2011.

claim: N-kinesins are motor proteins that drive anterograde transport on microtubules.
source: N-kinesins, the motor proteins that drive anterograde transport on microtubules, have also been reported to function in slow recycling (Hirokawa et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hirokawa et al., 2009.

claim: A kinesin-3 member KIF13A cooperates with RAB11A to generate and drive the peripheral transport of RE tubules.
source: A kinesin-3 member KIF13A cooperates with RAB11A to generate and drive the peripheral transport of RE tubules (Delevoye et al., 2014; Nakagawa et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Delevoye et al., 2014 and Nakagawa et al., 2000.

claim: KIF13A is essential for cargo delivery from RE to maturing melanosomes in melanocytes.
source: In addition, KIF13A is essential for cargo delivery from RE to maturing melanosomes in melanocytes (Delevoye et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Delevoye et al., 2009.

claim: KIF16B functions in regulating the motility of early endosomes and degradation of EGF receptor.
source: KIF16B, another member of kinesin-3, functions in regulating the motility of early endosomes and degradation of EGF receptor, and in the transcytosis of transferrin receptor (TfR) in polarized epithelial cells (Hoepfner et al., 2005; Perez Bay et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hoepfner et al., 2005 and Perez Bay et al., 2013.

claim: KIF16B functions in the transcytosis of transferrin receptor in polarized epithelial cells.
source: KIF16B, another member of kinesin-3, functions in regulating the motility of early endosomes and degradation of EGF receptor, and in the transcytosis of transferrin receptor (TfR) in polarized epithelial cells (Hoepfner et al., 2005; Perez Bay et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hoepfner et al., 2005 and Perez Bay et al., 2013.

claim: A kinesin-2 member KIF3B has been implicated in the recycling of TfR through the interaction with RAB11-FIP5.
source: A kinesin-2 member KIF3B has also been implicated in the recycling of TfR through the interaction with RAB11-FIP5 (Schonteich et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schonteich et al., 2008.

claim: Liver-specific Bloc1s1 knockout mice exhibit reduced LDLR in the liver and elevated plasma LDL levels due to alternative lysosome degradation of LDLR after impaired endocytic recycling.
source: Consequently, liver-specific Bloc1s1 knockout mice exhibit reduced LDLR in the liver and elevated plasma LDL levels due to alternative lysosome degradation of LDLR after impaired endocytic recycling.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is supported by experimental data.

claim: ApoE is a core protein component of very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) and high-density lipoprotein (HDL).
source: ApoE is a core protein component of very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) and high-density lipoprotein (HDL).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about lipoprotein composition.

claim: ApoB is a common constituent of LDL and VLDL.
source: Despite the reduced VLDL content, a common constituent of LDL and VLDL, ApoB, was significantly increased in cKO mouse plasma (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a), suggesting that increase of LDL in cKO mouse plasma was likely the main effect of BLOS1 deficiency on lipoproteins.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about lipoprotein composition.

claim: VLDL is largely converted to LDL in plasma.
source: VLDL is largely converted to LDL in plasma.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about lipoprotein metabolism.

claim: Liver is the primary site for plasma LDL clearance.
source: Liver is the primary site for plasma LDL clearance, the accumulation of LDL in cKO mouse plasma suggested that LDL clearance by cKO mouse liver could be impaired.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about LDL metabolism.

claim: Residues 76–100 on BLOS1 interacts with the cytosolic domain of LDLR at the C-terminus.
source: Taken together, these results showed that loss of BLOS1 in liver could lead to impaired LDL clearance from plasma which is caused by excessive lysosomal degradation of LDLR, and residues 76–100 on BLOS1 interacts with the cytosolic domain of LDLR at the C-terminus.
evidence: The claim is supported by GST pull-down experiments with BLOS1 truncations.

claim: Members of the heterodimeric kinesin-2 subfamily switch protofilaments during their processive movements.
source: In addition, members of the heterodimeric kinesin-2 subfamily switch protofilaments during their processive movements, which may contribute to the overcoming of microtubule obstacles (Brunnbauer et al., 2012; Hoeprich et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brunnbauer et al., 2012 and Hoeprich et al., 2017.

claim: Off-axis mode motion of cargoes were observed at microtubule intersections in vivo.
source: Such off-axis mode motion of cargoes were also observed at microtubule intersections in vivo (Verdeny-Vilanova et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Verdeny-Vilanova et al., 2017.

claim: Microtubule intersections serve as important sites for direction determination during cargo transport.
source: It has been reported that cargoes (lysosomes) pause at intersection points between multiple microtubules and switch to another microtubule track at some specific intersections, and these microtubule intersections serve as important sites for direction determination during cargo transport (Bálint et al., 2013; Bergman et al., 2018; Verdeny-Vilanova et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bálint et al., 2013, Bergman et al., 2018, and Verdeny-Vilanova et al., 2017.

claim: Cargoes pause at intersection points between multiple microtubules and switch to another microtubule track at some specific intersections.
source: It has been reported that cargoes (lysosomes) pause at intersection points between multiple microtubules and switch to another microtubule track at some specific intersections, and these microtubule intersections serve as important sites for direction determination during cargo transport (Bálint et al., 2013; Bergman et al., 2018; Verdeny-Vilanova et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bálint et al., 2013, Bergman et al., 2018, and Verdeny-Vilanova et al., 2017.
